title: Is recycling doing what we think?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: The council's audit says about a fifth of what goes in the recycling bin ends up incinerated anyway. Contamination, mostly.

turns.speaker: Rob
turns.text: A fifth. And people are washing yoghurt pots for that.

turns.speaker: Nick
turns.text: Washing them in hot water, which has its own footprint. There's a point where the effort costs more than it saves.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: For plastic, honestly, a lot of it never worked. Glass, paper, aluminium, those genuinely recycle. Aluminium is the one that actually pays for itself.

turns.speaker: Rob
turns.text: Because melting it is a fraction of the energy of making it new.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: About five per cent. Which is why it's the only one with a real market behind it.

turns.speaker: Nick
turns.text: The uncomfortable part is that recycling was promoted hardest by the people selling the packaging.

turns.speaker: Nick
turns.text: It's documented, though. If the container is recyclable then the problem is your sorting, not their product.

turns.speaker: Nick
turns.text: It moves the responsibility one step down, to you, at the kitchen bin.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Which is why deposit return works better than kerbside. Same bottle, but suddenly it's worth something.

turns.speaker: Rob
turns.text: Ninety per cent return rates in the countries that do it, isn't it.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Roughly, yes. It turns out people respond to money more reliably than to guilt.

points: A council audit found about a fifth of recycling is incinerated due to contamination.
Nick notes washing containers in hot water has its own footprint, so effort can exceed benefit.
Amira distinguishes materials: glass, paper and aluminium recycle genuinely, while much plastic never did.
Aluminium pays for itself because remelting uses roughly five per cent of the energy of new production.
Nick argues recycling was promoted by packaging producers because it shifts responsibility to the household.
They agree deposit return schemes outperform kerbside collection, achieving around ninety per cent returns, because people respond to money more reliably than to guilt.
